A single node typically tops out around 100 million vectors, but this is a rough ceiling rather than a hard target — the real limit depends heavily on dimensionality, datatype, and whether you're using quantization, so a 3072-dimension float32 collection will hit it far sooner than a 384-dimension uint8 one [c1]. Node count beyond this sanity check is also driven by fault-tolerance needs: for high availability in production, Qdrant recommends at least three nodes and a replication factor of two or higher [c1].

Qdrant returns HTTP 507 (Insufficient Storage) — or `ResourceExhausted` for gRPC clients — when a configured disk usage quota blocks writes [c5].

You can fix this by increasing the limit of open files allowed. For example, when launching via Docker, set the ulimit at container start:

```
docker run --ulimit nofile=10000:10000 qdrant/qdrant:latest
```

This sets both the soft and hard limits to 10000 [c1]. If you're not using Docker, you can instead run `ulimit -n 10000` for the current user session — but note this must be executed *before* starting the Qdrant server [c1].

This happens when each node doesn't have its own separate storage directory, volume, or mount — the WAL files are unavailable because they're already in use by another Qdrant instance accessing the same storage. The cluster handles sharing data between nodes itself, so each node (whether using Kubernetes, Docker, or running Qdrant directly) needs its own distinct storage location [c1].
You can return a response of "Accepted" (HTTP 202) right away and process the file as a background task, defining it to run after the response is returned [c1].

When `BackgroundTasks` is declared at multiple levels—such as in a dependency and in the path operation function—FastAPI knows how to reuse the same object, so all the background tasks from each level are merged together and run in the background after the response is sent [c1].

You should use Celery instead of FastAPI's built-in `BackgroundTasks` when you need to perform heavy background computation that doesn't necessarily need to run in the same process (i.e., you don't need to share memory, variables, etc.), and especially when you need to run background tasks across multiple processes or multiple servers. Celery requires more complex configuration, including a message/job queue manager like RabbitMQ or Redis. By contrast, if you just need to access variables and objects from the same FastAPI app or perform small background tasks (like sending an email notification), `BackgroundTasks` is sufficient [c1].
